extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter introducing vector spaces, matrices, eigenvalues/eigenvectors, Jordan form, and related structural theorems aimed at building conceptual understanding (basis-free viewpoint) and computational encodings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-dimensional vector spaces are isomorphic to k^n
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 9.5.3: If V is an n-dimensional vector space, then V ≅ k^{⊕n}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notion of isomorphism cares only about the size of a basis; it explains why many different n-dimensional spaces are structurally the same as k^n, though one may keep other 'essence' (e.g., polynomials vs coordinate tuples) for intuition or convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete isomorphism via coordinates (polynomials ↔ tuples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: V the real polynomials of degree ≤2; the map (a,b,c) ↦ ax^2 + bx + c is an isomorphism; evaluation at a point is a linear map (e.g., ax^2+bx+c ↦ 9a+3b+c is 'evaluation at 3').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use coordinate maps to concretely represent abstract vector spaces; evaluation maps are canonical simple examples of linear maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation maps are linear
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples (e) and (f): The map V→R by ax^2+bx+c ↦ 9a+3b+c (evaluation at 3) and W→R by f ↦ f(0) are linear maps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation at a fixed input is a straightforward linear functional; use such examples to ground the abstract definition of linear maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix is the encoding of a linear map relative to bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 9.6.1 and general discussion: given bases e1,...,em of V and w1,...,wn of W, the matrix of T:V→W is formed by writing each T(ej) in the basis of W and arranging those coordinate column vectors as the columns of an n×m array.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A matrix is the 'laziest possible way' to specify a linear map. The entries are just the coordinates of images of basis vectors; choosing different bases changes the matrix representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix multiplication corresponds to composition of linear maps
rubrics_metrics.description: If T:U→V and S:V→W have matrices (in chosen bases), then the matrix encoding of S∘T equals the product of the matrices of S and T (matrix multiplication rule derived from composing columnwise action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matrix multiplication is not an arbitrary recipe: it is the arithmetic that encodes composition. Examples with 2×2 matrices illustrate this derivation explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity matrix columns are images of basis vectors under identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Remark 9.6.2: The columns of the identity matrix are id(e1), id(e2), ... — e1, e2, ... respectively, hence the identity matrix is [1 0; 0 1] in 2×2 case because id sends the basis vectors to themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a natural basis-free reason for the familiar form of the identity matrix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrices depend on choice of basis (similarity = change of basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion / Pedagogical digression: matrices are encodings that depend on bases; T2 = S T1 S^{-1} is just rewriting the same linear map with a different choice of basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize basis-free viewpoint: the numbers in a matrix are not intrinsic, they represent the same map under chosen coordinates. This explains invariance properties like trace/determinant for similarity classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of subspace (submodule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 9.7.1: Let M be a left R-module. A submodule N of M is a module N such that every element of N is also an element of M. If M is a vector space then N is called a subspace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard closure-under-addition-and-scaling criterion; for vector spaces this is phrased in field-scaling language, and for modules the analogous generating set language is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kernel is a subspace
rubrics_metrics.description: Example 9.7.2: The kernel ker T = {v ∈ V | T(v) = 0_W} is a subspace of V because it is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use kernel to study injectivity and structure of linear maps; kernels are fundamental invariant subspaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Span of vectors is a subspace
rubrics_metrics.description: Example 9.7.3: For vectors v1,...,vm, their span {a1 v1 + ... + am vm | ai∈k} is a subspace of V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spans provide the canonical smallest subspace containing given vectors; useful when constructing bases or generating sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis completion (extend/contract bases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 9.7.5: If V is n-dimensional and V' a subspace with basis e1,...,em, then there exist em+1,...,en in V such that e1,...,en is a basis of V. In particular V' is finite-dimensional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can extend bases of subspaces to bases of the whole space; conversely, spanning sets can be reduced to bases. This is a key tool for constructing convenient bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picking convenient bases for linear maps (rank decomposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 9.7.6: For T:V→W finite-dimensional (dim V = n, dim W = m) there exist bases e1,...,en of V and f1,...,fm of W and an integer k≥0 such that T(ei)=fi for i≤k and T(ei)=0_W for i>k. Moreover dim ker T = n−k and dim im T = k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theorem gives the standard picture: V = ker T ⊕ V' where T annihilates ker T and is injective on V', sending it isomorphically into im T. It underlies the proof of rank-nullity and explains how to choose bases to simplify the matrix of T.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank-nullity theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 9.7.7: For finite-dimensional V and W and T:V→W, dim V = dim ker T + dim im T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow from Theorem 9.7.6; fundamental invariant relation linking dimension, kernel, and image (rank + nullity = dimension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lagrange interpolation as linear-algebraic fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 9.8.1: Given distinct x1,...,xn+1 and any y1,...,yn+1 there exists a unique polynomial P of degree ≤ n with P(xi)=yi for all i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the linear map T:V→R^{n+1} sending P to (P(x1),...,P(x_{n+1})); since dim V = n+1 = dim R^{n+1} and T is injective, it is bijective. This demonstrates solving interpolation via linear algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viewpoint: arrays of numbers are encodings, not the main objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedagogical digression (§9.9): The matrix is an encoding of a linear map; treating arrays as the primary objects hides conceptual meaning and leads to confusion about invariants like determinant/trace/characteristic polynomial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer basis-free definitions when possible and use matrices as concrete encodings for computation and proof; this gives clearer conceptual understanding of similarity, invariants, and theorems like Cayley–Hamilton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module notions: finitely generated and free modules
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions 9.10.1–9.10.2: An R-module M is finitely generated if it has a finite generating set. M is free if it has a basis; rank denotes size of a basis and then M ≅ R^{⊕n}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over general rings many vector-space theorems fail; examples (e.g., Z as Z-module) show bases may not exist. Use generating sets vs bases vocabulary appropriately; example Z[√2] is a free Z-module of rank 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of eigenvector and eigenvalue
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 10.3.1: For T:V→V and nonzero v∈V, v is an eigenvector if T(v)=λ v for some scalar λ∈k; λ is an eigenvalue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eigenvectors capture directions preserved up to scaling. Eigenspaces (together with 0) form subspaces and are central to simplifying the action of T.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eigenvalues may not exist over non-algebraically-closed fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Example 10.3.5: The 90° rotation map on R^2 has no eigenvectors (other than 0); eigenvalues need not exist over R. Theorem 10.3.6: Over an algebraically closed field and finite-dimensional V, an eigenvalue exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working over algebraically closed fields (e.g., C) every linear operator on a finite-dimensional space has at least one eigenvalue; proof uses polynomials in T and existence of roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jordan canonical form (existence and uniqueness up to block order)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 10.4.2: For T:V→V on a finite-dimensional vector space over an algebraically closed field, one can choose a basis so that the matrix is block-diagonal with Jordan blocks; this Jordan form is unique up to rearranging blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: V decomposes into direct sum of invariant subspaces J_i on which T acts as Jordan blocks. Diagonal matrices are the special case when all blocks are 1×1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nilpotent maps and staircase (Jordan) structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 10.5.1 and Theorem 10.5.5: T is nilpotent if T^m=0 for some m. Every nilpotent linear map on a finite-dimensional space decomposes into independent 'staircases' (chains v, T(v), T^2(v),...), giving Jordan blocks with zero eigenvalue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nilpotent Jordan structure: represent nilpotent operators as direct sums of descending staircases; this is the template used to build the full Jordan form by shifting by λ (i.e., S+λ id).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariant subspaces, indecomposable maps, and decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 10.6.1/10.6.2 and Proposition 10.6.3: A subspace W is T-invariant if T(w)∈W. T is indecomposable if V cannot be written as direct sum of two nontrivial T-invariant spaces. Any finite-dimensional V decomposes as V=V1⊕...⊕Vm where each Vi is T-invariant and T:Vi→Vi is indecomposable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decomposition reduces study of T to indecomposable pieces; each indecomposable piece yields a single Jordan block after shifting by an eigenvalue and applying nilpotent Jordan analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic vs geometric multiplicity (generalized eigenspace)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 10.8.2 and Proposition 10.8.4: Geometric multiplicity of λ is dim of the λ-eigenspace (true eigenvectors). Generalized eigenspace V^λ = {v | (T−λ id)^n(v)=0 for some n}; algebraic multiplicity is dim V^λ. In Jordan form: geometric multiplicity = number of Jordan blocks for λ; algebraic multiplicity = sum of sizes of those blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric multiplicity ≤ algebraic multiplicity. These notions distinguish number of independent eigenvectors from total multiplicity of λ in characteristic polynomial / Jordan blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace and determinant via eigenvalues (with algebraic multiplicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition (10.8): The trace is the sum of eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity, and the determinant is the product of eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This intrinsic description ties numerical invariants to spectral data but relies on working over an algebraically closed field; alternate computational definitions exist that avoid this assumption.
